paras: The attempted lynching of Laurie Davis took place in late April or early May 1888 near Spencer's Store, Virginia, when friends of W. D. Smith, a Stokes county, North Carolina, tobacco peddler, captured Davis, a Black man accused of shooting Smith. According to the Western Sentinel of Winston-Salem, some of the captors had to be restrained from lynching him, and he was instead jailed at Danbury to await requisition by the Governor of South Carolina.

On April 26, 1888, the Sentinel reported that Smith, "a well known tobacco peddler" of Stokes county, had been shot and robbed near Columbia, South Carolina, "a few days ago by his negro driver." Smith was described as seriously wounded with "but little hope of his recovery," and the driver was said to have escaped with $185 taken from him. That first item did not name the driver.

Two weeks later the paper identified Laurie Davis as "the negro who shot W. D. Smith" and reported that he had been captured near Spencer's Store, Virginia, "one day last week by some of Smith's friends." "It was all that some of the cooler heads could do," the paper wrote, "to prevent the negro from being lynched." The account gives no number for the captors and describes no specific act toward a lynching.

Davis was then held in jail at Danbury, the Stokes county town, "subject to the requisition of the Governor of South Carolina." No report of his return to South Carolina, a trial, or Smith's fate appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from two short local items in the Western Sentinel of Winston-Salem, which identified Smith as a man "of Stokes" and noted that it had reported the shooting earlier. The April item ran under the heading "Shot and Robbed," while the May paragraph on the capture appeared without a headline beneath a notice of the Salem Academy commencement. Both items treated the accusation as established, identifying the accused only as "his negro driver" and "the negro," and the paper credited "cooler heads" for averting the lynching without otherwise commenting on it.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Laurie Davis
bases: Friends of the wounded man captured the accused and, by the paper's account, nearly lynched him before cooler heads intervened; he was then jailed (A2).

No one was killed: Davis was captured and, according to the only account, saved from lynching by 'cooler heads' and lodged in jail at Danbury (A2). The captors were 'some of Smith's friends', a private group of unstated size acting on the shooting accusation (A2).
The capture and near-lynching appear only in one paragraph of the Western Sentinel (A2); the paper's earlier item on the shooting (A1) is from the same paper and does not name the driver.

accounts.label: Western Sentinel local report
accounts.gist: Smith's negro driver shot and robbed him near Columbia, S.C., and escaped; two weeks later the paper named Laurie Davis as the man who shot Smith and reported his capture in Virginia, a narrowly averted lynching, and his jailing at Danbury.

framing.detail: A short unheadlined local paragraph calls Davis 'the negro who shot W. D. Smith', treating the accusation as fact, and credits 'cooler heads' with preventing the lynching without further comment.

conflicts.note: Not a true contradiction: the later item refers back to the earlier 'mention', but only it names the driver as Laurie Davis.
